content.title: About
content.content: Chorizo is a traditional Spanish sausage made from pork, seasoned with paprika, garlic, and other spices. It has a bright red color, a flavorful slightly spicy taste, and a firm yet tender texture. Chorizo can be eaten raw, fried, stewed, or used in dishes such as paella, beans with chorizo, and sandwiches.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: There are several regional varieties: Andalusian (soft, smoked), Castilian (dry, spicier) and Leonese (often with wine).
The traditional paprika used is called “pimentón” and comes in sweet, semi‑sweet, or hot versions.
Chorizo is often smoked over oak or beech wood, giving it a distinctive aroma.
Mexico has its own version of chorizo, made with beef and a wetter texture than the Spanish type.
In Spain chorizo is commonly served as tapas, sliced thinly.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Pork in chorizo provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Chorizo contains heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It supplies B1, B3, B6 and B12 vitamins that support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Beneficial fats
items.content: While chorizo is fatty, part of its fat is monounsaturated and polyunsaturated, which can be beneficial in moderation.

items.title: Antioxidants from paprika
items.content: Paprika adds carotenoids and vitamin C, providing antioxidant properties.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Chorizo is often salty; excess sodium may raise blood pressure.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: A large portion of its fat is saturated, which in excess can contribute to cardiovascular disease.

items.title: Pork allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic or intolerant to pork.

items.title: Preservatives and nitrites
items.content: Some commercial chorizo contain additives that can be unsafe in large amounts.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice chorizo thinly for a snack, add it to omelets, pasta, stews, paella, or bake it in the oven. It is often pan‑fried first to release its aromatic fats.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep chorizo in the refrigerator in an airtight container for up to 2 weeks. For longer storage freeze it in a sealed bag for up to 3 months. Before use check for off‑odors or discoloration; discard if any signs of spoilage appear.
